phenomenon.name: Aokigahara
phenomenon.subcategory: Forest associated with Japanese folklore and modern psychogeography

description.summary: A dense forest at the northwestern foot of Mount Fuji in Yamanashi Prefecture, Japan, grown on the lava flow of the 864 CE Jōgan eruption and associated in modern reputation with yūrei folklore and a high incidence of suicide.
description.full: Aokigahara (青木ヶ原), also called Jukai (樹海, 'Sea of Trees'), is a roughly 30 km² (≈12 sq mi) forest at the northwestern foot of Mount Fuji in Yamanashi Prefecture, Japan. The forest grew on the Aokigahara lava flow produced by the 864 CE Jōgan eruption of Mount Fuji's flank vents (in particular Mount Nagao). Its substrate of porous basalt, weak compass-disturbing magnetic anomalies in places, dense undergrowth and acoustic dampening have given the forest a reputation for disorientation. Aokigahara is associated in Japanese folklore with yūrei (restless ghosts) and is the setting of Seichō Matsumoto's 1960 novel 'Tower of Waves' (Nami no Tō), which is widely credited with shaping its modern reputation. From the late 20th century onward Aokigahara has become widely known internationally as a site of suicide; Japanese authorities and volunteer organisations conduct annual sweeps and have installed signs encouraging visitors to seek help. In 2017 the forest gained additional global notoriety when American YouTuber Logan Paul uploaded a video showing a deceased person filmed inside the forest, prompting widespread condemnation and changes to YouTube's policies. Conservationists, mental-health advocates, and local communities increasingly object to sensationalised 'suicide forest' framings, emphasising Aokigahara's ecological, geological, and cultural significance.

etymology.origin: Japanese 青木ヶ原 (Aokigahara): 'aoki' (青木) is the green-leaved shrub Aucuba japonica; 'ga' is a possessive particle; 'hara' (原) means 'plain' or 'field'.
etymology.meaning: Approximately 'Aokigi (Aucuba) plain'; commonly rendered loosely as 'sea of green trees'. The compound Jukai (樹海) means 'sea of trees'.
etymology.first_use: Place name long established in Edo-period and modern Japanese gazetteers.

taxonomy.subtype: Lava-flow forest with reputed paranormal associations

related_phenomena.description: Japanese restless ghosts, traditionally associated with the forest

related_phenomena.name: Suicide-site folklore
related_phenomena.description: Comparable global folklore around sites of self-harm

features.description: Forest grows directly on the porous basaltic Aokigahara lava flow of 864 CE
Year-round dense vegetation that absorbs sound and limits visibility
Numerous lava caves and tubes, including Narusawa Ice Cave and Fugaku Wind Cave, are accessible within or beside the forest
Localised magnetic anomalies in the basalt can disturb compasses (popularly exaggerated)

physical.morphology: Temperate volcanic forest of pine, hemlock, and Aucuba japonica, on basalt with shallow, irregular soils.

range.description: A single contiguous forest at the northwestern base of Mount Fuji.

hotspots.name: Aokigahara forest core

location.description: Forest at the northwestern foot of Mount Fuji

hotspots.notes: Approximate coordinates for the centre of the Aokigahara lava flow.

first_recorded.source: Heian-period accounts of the Jōgan eruption of Mount Fuji

peak_activity_periods.description: Publication of Seichō Matsumoto's 'Tower of Waves' fixes the forest in popular imagination
Widely cited statistic that 105 bodies were recovered from the forest in 2003
International controversy over Logan Paul video filmed in Aokigahara

origins.cultural_roots: Japanese folk-religious associations of dense forest, mountain, and volcanic landscape with yūrei and kami; Mount Fuji's standing as a sacred mountain.
origins.earliest_accounts: The 864 CE Jōgan eruption of Mount Fuji's flank vents produced the Aokigahara lava flow on which the forest later grew.
origins.folklore_connections: Yūrei traditions; the historical tradition of ubasute (the abandonment of the elderly), often invoked in connection with Aokigahara, is regarded by historians as more legend than documented practice.

timeline.event: Jōgan eruption of Mount Fuji creates the Aokigahara lava flow
timeline.significance: Geological origin of the forest substrate

timeline.event: Seichō Matsumoto publishes the novel 'Nami no Tō' (Tower of Waves), set in part in Aokigahara
timeline.significance: Often credited with consolidating the forest's modern reputation

timeline.event: Wataru Tsurumi publishes 'The Complete Manual of Suicide' (Kanzen Jisatsu Manyuaru), which mentions Aokigahara
Local authorities report 105 bodies recovered from the forest in 2003
timeline.significance: Widely cited datum in international coverage
timeline.source: Yamanashi Prefectural Police; reported in Wikipedia: Aokigahara

timeline.event: Logan Paul uploads a YouTube video filmed inside Aokigahara showing a deceased person
timeline.significance: International controversy; YouTube subsequently revises monetisation policies and removes Paul from preferred ad programs

history.modern_era: Aokigahara is administered as part of the Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park. Local government, NPOs, and forestry workers conduct annual body-recovery sweeps and prevention work; signs at trailheads encourage visitors in distress to seek help. Yamanashi authorities have stopped publishing annual suicide statistics for the forest in an effort to reduce 'cluster' effects.

documentary.name: Tower of Waves (Nami no Tō)
documentary.description: Seichō Matsumoto's novel; one of the principal cultural shapers of Aokigahara's modern reputation.

paranormal.name: Yūrei haunting
paranormal.description: Folkloric framing in which the forest is haunted by yūrei, the restless dead, with the forest atmosphere amplifying perception of supernatural presence.
evidence_cited: Folk reports of strange sounds and disorientation
Cultural framing in literature and film

skeptical.name: Reputation effect
skeptical.description: Aokigahara's reputation has been amplified by literature (Matsumoto 1960), self-help / reference works (Tsurumi 1993), and global media (Logan Paul 2017), creating a feedback loop that drives further visits and reporting.
evidence_cited: Documented role of media in suicide-cluster effects
Yamanashi Prefecture's deliberate decision to stop publishing forest-specific suicide statistics

skeptical.name: Geophysical disorientation
skeptical.description: Reports of compasses misbehaving and easy disorientation are partly explained by localised magnetic anomalies in basalt and by the forest's acoustic dampening and uniform terrain.
evidence_cited: Magnetic surveys of the lava flow

stories: Folk associations of Aokigahara with yūrei and lost travellers
folklore.beliefs: The forest is regarded by many local residents and Japanese cultural commentators as deserving respect rather than sensationalism.

literature: Tower of Waves (Nami no Tō) — Seichō Matsumoto (1960)
The Complete Manual of Suicide — Wataru Tsurumi (1993, Japanese)
other: Yamanashi Prefecture trailhead signs encouraging visitors in distress to seek help

organizations.focus: Mental-health support and crisis line in Japan

research.ongoing_studies: Continuing public-health research on suicide prevention in Japan; Yamanashi authorities have curtailed publication of forest-specific statistics to reduce cluster effects.
